items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the actual land on which a settlement is built”.
items.answer: Site

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the actual land on which a settlement is built”.
items.answer: Site

items.stem: Explain the difference between the site and the situation of a settlement.
items.answer: Site is the land the settlement is built on (e.g. a dry-point above a flood plain); situation is its location relative to surrounding features such as routes, rivers and other settlements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 2.1, a description of the site of a market town. The town grew around a castle on a small hill beside a river, at the lowest point where the river could be bridged. Roads from four directions meet at the bridge, and a railway runs through a gap in the hills. Suggest two functions the town might have today.
items.answer: Market town; service centre for surrounding villages; tourism (castle); commuter town; light industry.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 describes part of a 1:50 000 map. Town M lies at a point where a river is crossed by two main roads; the old centre is on a low hill 20 m above the flood plain; a castle stands on the hill. The river is narrow here and is crossed by an old stone bridge. Railway and roads follow the valley through a gap in a ridge to the north. (a) Explain why a bridging point is a good site for a settlement. (b) Suggest two functions the town might have today.
items.answer: (a) Routes converge to cross the river, bringing trade and travellers; markets grow there. (b) Market town; service centre for surrounding villages; tourism (castle); commuter town; light industry.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark routes converge; 1 mark trade [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 2.1 shows the population and number of services in settlements in one region. City: population 667 000, 585 services. Large town: population 111 000, 154 services. Small town: population 24 000, 108 services. Village: population 600, 14 services. Hamlet: population 50, 3 services. (a) Calculate the number of people per service in the small town. (b) Explain why the city has services not found in the small town.
items.answer: (a) about 222 people per service (b) High-order services (hospital, university, department stores) have large thresholds that only a large population can support, and people will travel far for them.
items.markingKey: (a) 24 000 ÷ 108 = 222.2 [1] (b) 1 mark threshold; 1 mark range [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 describes part of a 1:50 000 map. Town M lies at a point where a river is crossed by two main roads; the old centre is on a low hill 20 m above the flood plain; a castle stands on the hill. The river is narrow here and is crossed by an old stone bridge. Railway and roads follow the valley through a gap in a ridge to the north. (a) Identify three site or situation factors that helped the town to grow. (b) Suggest two functions the town might have today.
items.answer: (a) Any three: defensive hill with castle; dry-point site above flood plain; bridging point; route centre where roads meet; gap through the ridge; water supply from the river. (b) Market town; service centre for surrounding villages; tourism (castle); commuter town; light industry.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the commercial centre of a city with shops, offices, banks and high land values”.
items.answer: Central business district (CBD)
items.markingKey: Central business district (CBD): the commercial centre of a city with shops, offices, banks and high land values. [1]

items.stem: Explain why land values fall with distance from the CBD.
items.answer: The CBD is the most accessible point, so demand for land from shops and offices is highest; further out accessibility falls, so less is paid and land uses change to housing and then farming.
items.markingKey: 1 mark accessibility; 1 mark competition/demand [2]

items.stem: Explain why many CBDs have declined.
items.answer: Out-of-town shopping centres with free parking, online shopping, congestion and high rents in the CBD; offices moving to business parks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.answer: CBD at 0 km; suburbs or rural-urban fringe at 8 km.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities”.
items.answer: Urbanisation
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: the increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: Explain why informal settlements develop in LIC cities.
items.answer: Rapid rural-urban migration and natural increase create demand for housing that the city cannot meet; migrants are poor and cannot afford formal housing, so they build on unused land on hillsides, flood plains or by railways.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rapid growth; 1 mark poverty/cost; 1 mark unused land [3]

items.stem: Describe the problems faced by people living in informal settlements.
items.answer: Overcrowding; lack of clean water and sanitation; disease; fire and flood risk; insecure tenure and eviction; crime; long journeys to work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: For Dharavi, Mumbai, India or another example of an informal settlement in an LIC or MIC city, briefly evaluate attempts to improve the settlement.
items.answer: Dharavi, Mumbai, India: The Dharavi Redevelopment Project plans to rehouse residents in high-rise blocks with free flats for eligible families and to build commercial space; critics fear loss of businesses and community ties, and many residents are not eligible.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named schemes (upgrading, rehousing, self-help), what has worked and what has not, judgement. [4]

items.stem: For Rocinha, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil or another example of an informal settlement in an LIC or MIC city, briefly evaluate attempts to improve the settlement.
items.answer: Rocinha, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: The Favela-Bairro project upgraded favelas with paved roads, water, sewers and health centres; police pacification units (from 2008); a cable car was built in the nearby Complexo do Alemão; results have been mixed because of funding cuts and continuing violence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named schemes (upgrading, rehousing, self-help), what has worked and what has not, judgement. [4]

items.stem: Name one example of an informal settlement in an LIC or MIC city you have studied and, for that example, describe the living conditions in the settlement.
items.answer: Rocinha, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: Brazil’s largest favela, with about 70 000-100 000 people (estimates vary) on a steep hillside; houses built of brick and concrete by residents; poor sanitation and landslide risk; drug gangs and crime; but many shops, services and a strong community.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Housing, density, water and sanitation, health, employment (formal/informal), with figures. [4]

items.answer: (a) 281% (b) Informal settlements, shortage of housing, water and sanitation, traffic congestion, air pollution, unemployment and informal jobs.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the increase in the area or total population of towns and cities”.
items.answer: Urban growth
items.markingKey: Urban growth: the increase in the area or total population of towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Informal settlements have no economic activity.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many have thriving informal economies; Dharavi has thousands of small businesses such as recycling, pottery and leatherwork.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why urbanisation is happening faster in LICs than HICs.
items.answer: LICs are urbanising rapidly because of rural poverty and high natural increase among young urban populations; HICs are already highly urbanised (about 80%).
items.markingKey: 1 mark migration; 1 mark natural increase; 1 mark HICs already urban [3]

items.stem: Explain how self-help schemes improve informal settlements.
items.answer: Residents are given low-cost loans, materials or legal ownership, so they upgrade their own homes with brick walls, water and sanitation; cheap and keeps communities together.
items.markingKey: 1 mark how; 1 mark benefit [2]

items.stem: Table 2.3 shows population data for Country Q. 1980: total population 34 million, 28% urban. 2000: total population 50 million, 39% urban. 2020: total population 80 million, 54% urban. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in urban population from 1980 to 2020. (b) Explain the difference between urbanisation and urban growth, using the data.
items.answer: (a) 354.7% (b) Urbanisation is the rise in the urban share (28% to 54%); urban growth is the rise in the number of urban people (9.5 to 43.2 million).

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “when there are too many vehicles for the road space, causing slow journeys”.
items.answer: Traffic congestion
items.markingKey: Traffic congestion: when there are too many vehicles for the road space, causing slow journeys. [1]

items.stem: Explain the causes of traffic congestion in cities.
items.answer: Rising car ownership; many people commuting into the CBD at the same times; narrow old streets; poor or overcrowded public transport; road works and deliveries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Explain how a bus rapid transit system can make a city more sustainable.
items.answer: Dedicated lanes make buses fast and reliable, encouraging people to leave cars at home; fewer cars reduce congestion, fuel use and air pollution; cheap fares help the poor reach jobs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark how; 1 mark environmental benefit; 1 mark social benefit [3]

items.stem: Name one example of a sustainable urban scheme you have studied and, for that example, describe the strategies used to make the city more sustainable.
items.answer: London, UK: Congestion charge (2003) and Ultra Low Emission Zone (2019, expanded 2023); Oyster cards and an extensive Underground, bus and Overground network; cycle hire and superhighways; brownfield regeneration at Docklands and the Olympic Park in Stratford.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Transport, waste, green space, housing, energy – with named schemes and figures. [4]

items.stem: Explain why air pollution is a serious problem in many LIC and MIC cities.
items.answer: Rapid growth in old, poorly maintained vehicles; factories with few controls; burning of waste and fuels for cooking; weak enforcement; in some cities the relief traps smog.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the problems of cities in LICs are more serious than the problems of cities in HICs. You may wish to consider: transport; pollution.
items.answer: For: LIC cities face informal settlements, lack of clean water and sanitation, disease and rapid unplanned growth (e.g. Kibera, Dharavi). Against: HIC cities have serious congestion, air pollution, homelessness, inequality and ageing infrastructure. Some LIC/MIC cities (Curitiba) have found sustainable solutions. Judgement: Problems in LIC cities are generally more severe because of their speed of growth and lack of money, but HIC cities also face major challenges.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the location of a settlement in relation to the surrounding area, such as rivers, routes and other settlements”.
items.answer: Situation
items.markingKey: Situation: the location of a settlement in relation to the surrounding area, such as rivers, routes and other settlements. [1]

items.stem: Explain why larger settlements have larger spheres of influence.
items.answer: They have more high-order services with large thresholds and ranges, so people travel further to use them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark more high-order services; 1 mark range [2]

items.stem: Compare land use patterns in cities in HICs and LICs.
items.answer: HICs: wealthy often live in suburbs and the poor in the inner city. LICs: wealthy live near the CBD in high-quality housing; poor live in informal settlements on the edge or on hazardous land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each; 1 mark comparison [3]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “urbanisation”?
options: An area of unplanned, often illegally built housing that lacks basic services (also called a squatter settlement or slum).
The increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities.
The increase in the area or total population of towns and cities.
A city with a population of more than 10 million.
items.answer: The increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities.
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: the increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Most urban growth in LICs now comes from natural increase as well as migration.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Young migrants have children in the city, so natural increase adds to growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why urbanisation is happening faster in LICs than HICs. (b) A revision website states: “Clearing informal settlements and building tower blocks always solves the housing problem.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) LICs are urbanising rapidly because of rural poverty and high natural increase among young urban populations; HICs are already highly urbanised (about 80%). (b) Not correct. Clearance breaks up communities and businesses, and rents may be too high for the poor.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark migration; 1 mark natural increase; 1 mark HICs already urban [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Building more roads always solves traffic congestion.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. New roads often attract more traffic (induced demand); public transport and demand management are often more effective.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the causes of the urban heat island effect.
items.answer: Concrete and tarmac absorb heat by day and release it at night; heat from buildings, vehicles and industry; fewer plants mean less evapotranspiration; pollution traps heat.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Study your case study of a sustainable urban scheme (for example Curitiba, Brazil). Briefly evaluate how successful the strategies have been.
items.answer: Curitiba, Brazil: Lower car use and pollution than other Brazilian cities, more green space and cheap transport for the poor; but the BRT has become overcrowded as the city has grown to about 1.9 million, and informal settlements still exist on the edge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Evidence of success and of continuing problems; judgement. [4]

items.stem: For Curitiba, Brazil or another example of a sustainable urban scheme, briefly describe the strategies used to make the city more sustainable.
items.answer: Curitiba, Brazil: A bus rapid transit system (from 1974) with dedicated lanes and “tube” stations carries over 1 million passengers a day; parks on flood-prone land; a “green exchange” in which poor residents swap recyclable waste for food or bus tickets; about 70% of waste recycled; pedestrianised centre.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Transport, waste, green space, housing, energy – with named schemes and figures. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the problems of cities in LICs are more serious than the problems of cities in HICs. You may wish to consider: pollution; informal settlements.
items.answer: For: LIC cities face informal settlements, lack of clean water and sanitation, disease and rapid unplanned growth (e.g. Kibera, Dharavi). Against: HIC cities have serious congestion, air pollution, homelessness, inequality and ageing infrastructure. Some LIC/MIC cities (Curitiba) have found sustainable solutions. Judgement: Problems in LIC cities are generally more severe because of their speed of growth and lack of money, but HIC cities also face major challenges.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the main economic activity or purpose of a settlement, such as a port, market town or tourist resort”.
items.answer: Function
items.markingKey: Function: the main economic activity or purpose of a settlement, such as a port, market town or tourist resort. [1]

items.stem: Explain why low-order services are found in almost every settlement.
items.answer: They have small thresholds and short ranges, so even a small population can support them and people will not travel far for everyday goods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark threshold; 1 mark range [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 2.1, a description of the site of a market town. The town grew around a castle on a small hill beside a river, at the lowest point where the river could be bridged. Roads from four directions meet at the bridge, and a railway runs through a gap in the hills. Explain why the town has a larger sphere of influence than nearby villages.
items.answer: It has more high-order services (supermarkets, secondary school, hospital) and good road links, so people travel further to use it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark services; 1 mark accessibility [2]

items.stem: Table 2.1 shows the population and number of services in settlements in one region. City: population 374 000, 848 services. Large town: population 131 000, 244 services. Small town: population 23 000, 46 services. Village: population 2 200, 25 services. Hamlet: population 90, 0 services. (a) Describe the relationship between population and number of services. (b) Explain why the city has services not found in the small town. (c) Suggest a suitable graph to show these data and explain your choice.
items.answer: (a) Positive: the city with 374 000 people has 848 services while the hamlet with 90 has 0. (b) High-order services (hospital, university, department stores) have large thresholds that only a large population can support, and people will travel far for them. (c) A scatter graph with logarithmic scales, because both values cover a very wide range and the aim is to show a relationship.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark positive; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark threshold; 1 mark range [2] (c) 1 mark scatter; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the outer residential areas of a city, often with lower-density housing built later”.
items.answer: Suburbs
items.markingKey: Suburbs: the outer residential areas of a city, often with lower-density housing built later. [1]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of building on brownfield sites.
items.answer: Advantages: reuses derelict land, protects countryside, services already present, regenerates the inner city. Disadvantages: may need costly decontamination and clearance; less space for gardens.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each side up to [3]

items.stem: Students carried out a transect from the centre of Jakarta to its edge. Table 2.2 shows land value ($ per m²) and the mean height of buildings (storeys). 0 km: $3000, 27 storeys. 1 km: $1950, 9 storeys. 2 km: $1390, 3 storeys. 3 km: $750, 3 storeys. 4 km: $370, 2 storeys. 6 km: $340, 2 storeys. 8 km: $80, 1 storey. Explain the link between land value and building height.
items.answer: Where land is expensive, developers build upwards to fit more floor space on a small plot; where land is cheap, buildings are low and spread out.
items.markingKey: 1 mark high value = tall; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Students carried out a transect from the centre of Accra to its edge. Table 2.2 shows land value ($ per m²) and the mean height of buildings (storeys). 0 km: $2000, 27 storeys. 1 km: $1260, 6 storeys. 2 km: $950, 5 storeys. 3 km: $460, 3 storeys. 4 km: $260, 2 storeys. 6 km: $130, 2 storeys. 8 km: $80, 1 storey. (a) State the first distance at which land value is half or less of the value at the centre. (b) Name the urban zone found at 0 km and the zone at 8 km.
items.answer: (a) 2 km ($950) (b) CBD at 0 km; suburbs or rural-urban fringe at 8 km.
items.markingKey: (a) half of 2000 = 1000 [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students carried out a transect from the centre of Lima to its edge. Table 2.2 shows land value ($ per m²) and the mean height of buildings (storeys). 0 km: $2000, 27 storeys. 1 km: $1390, 9 storeys. 2 km: $870, 3 storeys. 3 km: $430, 2 storeys. 4 km: $260, 2 storeys. 6 km: $200, 2 storeys. 8 km: $40, 1 storey. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in land value between 0 km and 2 km. (b) Name the urban zone found at 0 km and the zone at 8 km.
items.answer: (a) 56.5% (b) CBD at 0 km; suburbs or rural-urban fringe at 8 km.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “urban growth”?
options: A city with a population of more than 10 million.
An area of unplanned, often illegally built housing that lacks basic services (also called a squatter settlement or slum).
Jobs that are not officially recognised, taxed or regulated, such as street selling.
The increase in the area or total population of towns and cities.
items.answer: The increase in the area or total population of towns and cities.
items.markingKey: Urban growth: the increase in the area or total population of towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Clearing informal settlements and building tower blocks always solves the housing problem.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Clearance breaks up communities and businesses, and rents may be too high for the poor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why urbanisation is happening faster in LICs than HICs. (b) Explain how self-help schemes improve informal settlements.
items.answer: (a) LICs are urbanising rapidly because of rural poverty and high natural increase among young urban populations; HICs are already highly urbanised (about 80%). (b) Residents are given low-cost loans, materials or legal ownership, so they upgrade their own homes with brick walls, water and sanitation; cheap and keeps communities together.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark migration; 1 mark natural increase; 1 mark HICs already urban [3] (b) 1 mark how; 1 mark benefit [2]

items.stem: Table 2.3 shows population data for Country P. 1980: total population 34 million, 19% urban. 2000: total population 60 million, 32% urban. 2020: total population 88 million, 45% urban. Suggest two reasons for the changes shown.
items.answer: Rural-urban migration (push: poverty, lack of services; pull: jobs, services) and high natural increase in cities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of an informal settlement in an LIC or MIC city (for example Dharavi, Mumbai, India). Briefly describe the living conditions in the settlement.
items.answer: Dharavi, Mumbai, India: About 1 million people in about 2.1 km² – one of the highest densities in the world; many share one toilet between hundreds of people; open drains and water from standpipes for a few hours a day; but an estimated 5000 businesses and 15 000 one-room factories (recycling, pottery, leather, textiles) with output worth over US$600 million a year.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Housing, density, water and sanitation, health, employment (formal/informal), with figures. [4]

items.stem: With reference to Dharavi, Mumbai, India, or another example of an informal settlement in an LIC or MIC city you have studied, describe the living conditions in the settlement.
items.answer: Model answer (Dharavi, Mumbai, India): About 1 million people in about 2.1 km² – one of the highest densities in the world; many share one toilet between hundreds of people; open drains and water from standpipes for a few hours a day; but an estimated 5000 businesses and 15 000 one-room factories (recycling, pottery, leather, textiles) with output worth over US$600 million a year.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Housing, density, water and sanitation, health, employment (formal/informal), with figures. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Recycling and waste reduction help make cities more sustainable.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They save resources, energy and landfill space.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Urban problems only occur in LIC cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. HIC cities also have congestion, pollution, housing shortages and inequality.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A traffic count was carried out on a main road into the centre of Nairobi. Vehicles per hour: 07:00 642, 08:00 1074, 09:00 845, 10:00 482, 12:00 559, 14:00 503, 16:00 723, 17:00 1007, 18:00 813. (a) Describe the pattern of traffic through the day. (b) Calculate the mean number of vehicles per hour.
items.answer: (a) Two peaks: morning at 08:00 (1074) and evening at 17:00 (1007); lowest in the middle of the day (482). (b) 738.7
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark two peaks; 1 mark data [2] (b) 6648 ÷ 9 = 738.7 [2]

items.stem: A traffic count was carried out on a main road into the centre of Bogotá. Vehicles per hour: 07:00 682, 08:00 1321, 09:00 929, 10:00 617, 12:00 622, 14:00 620, 16:00 922, 17:00 1216, 18:00 933. (a) Suggest two strategies the city could use to reduce peak congestion. (b) Suggest how the reliability of the count could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Bus lanes or BRT; park and ride; congestion charge; staggered working hours or home working; cycle lanes. (b) Count on several different days and in different seasons, using the same length of count and site each time; use more than one counter.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: Name an example of a sustainable urban scheme. For your chosen example, evaluate how successful the strategies have been.
items.answer: Model answer (London, UK): Traffic in the charging zone fell by about 30% at first and air quality has improved; but congestion has returned because of delivery vans and taxis, and the charge is criticised as unfair to low-income drivers.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Evidence of success and of continuing problems; judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]
